chapter.title: The Classic Rexx Interface to SQLite
chapter.para: The classic Rexx interface to SQLite provides a complete functional inteface to SQLite. This allows the Rexx programmer who prefers to not program with objects the same access to the SQLite database engine as the object-orientated Rexx programmer.

The intent is for the classic Rexx interface to allow access to the complete functionality and feature set of SQLite. The first release of ooSQLite will not meet, and is not intended to meet, that goal. Lesser used functionality will be added over time.

The object-orientated and classic Rexx interfaces are developed in tandem. As each new feature or functionality of SQLite is added to ooSQLite, access to the feature is added to both interfaces at the same time. There is no SQLite functionality in the classic Rexx interface that can not be accessed through the object-orientated interface. And, vice versa.
The following table lists all of the routines used in the functional (classic Rexx) interface of the ooSQLite package:

section.title: &added11;Handles
section.para:
In the classic Rexx interface, database connections, prepared statements, online backups, and mutexes are handles: Pointer objects. ooSQLite keeps a record of every handle it returns, and of its kind, from the moment it returns it until SQLite frees what the handle refers to. These are the handles, and how long each one is valid:
A database connection, from oosqlOpen (also when it returns an error code, as long as the handle is not null) until oosqlClose returns OK. A close that returns BUSY leaves the connection open, and its handle valid.
A prepared statement, from oosqlPrepare until oosqlFinalize, whatever oosqlFinalize returns.
An online backup, from oosqlBackupInit until oosqlBackupFinish, whatever oosqlBackupFinish returns.
A mutex, from oosqlMutexAlloc until oosqlMutexFree. The mutex of a connection, returned by oosqlDbMutex, is valid while its connection is open: it can be entered, tried, and left, but not freed.
A value returned by oosqlColumnValue, or by the columnValue method of an ooSQLiteStmt object, until its statement is finalized.
The SQLite context and the values passed to a user defined function (see oosqlCreateFunction and createFunction), only during that invocation of the routine or method.

Every routine that takes a handle checks it, and so do the class methods of ooSQLResult and ooSQLValue, which take a context or a value. They raise a syntax error, 88.914, if the argument is not a Pointer object; 88.900 if it is a null handle, for example "Argument 1, the prepared statement handle, must not be null"; and 88.900 if the handle is not valid any more, or is of another kind, for example a statement handle where a connection is needed: "Argument 1, the database connection handle, is not a live database connection handle". The exceptions for null handles are oosqlFinalize, which does nothing, oosqlStmtBusy, which returns false, and oosqlNextStmt, which starts from the first statement, as for .nil.

The check has limits, and programs must still not use a handle once the routine that frees it has been called. ooSQLite recognizes a handle by its address. When SQLite frees an object and then creates another one of the same kind, it may place it at the same address: an old handle then refers to the new object, passes the check, and acts on that object. A value of oosqlColumnValue passes the check until its statement is finalized, but it is only valid while the statement stays on the same result row. Dropping the variable that holds a handle, as the examples do, prevents using it by mistake.

A handle can be shared by several threads. The routines that free a handle, oosqlFinalize, oosqlClose, oosqlBackupFinish, and oosqlMutexFree, wait while another thread is running a routine with that handle, or with a handle that belongs to it, such as a value of oosqlColumnValue for a statement. Then they free it, and the other threads get the syntax error described above the next time they use it. While oosqlClose closes a connection, the routines that other threads start with that connection wait to know whether it was closed or, if oosqlClose returns BUSY, is still open. A thread that is waiting to enter a mutex with oosqlMutexEnter is running a routine with it too, so oosqlMutexFree waits until that thread has entered the mutex and that routine has returned.

A thread never waits for itself: a callback routine can free a handle that the routine running the callback is using, with the same results as before. Two threads can still wait for each other for ever: for example, when callback routines running on two threads each free a handle that the other thread is using, or when a thread frees a mutex that it holds while another thread is waiting to enter it. Before ooSQLite 1.1, a handle checked by one thread could be freed by another thread before the first one used it, and the interpreter could crash.

In the object orientated interface, the methods of a connection or a statement object are guarded, so ooRexx runs them one at a time for each object, and a statement finalized by another thread raises a syntax error in the next method.
Before ooSQLite 1.1, only null handles were detected. A handle that was not valid any more, or was of another kind, had unpredictable results, and often crashed the interpreter.

section.title: Prepared Statements
section.para:
In the classic Rexx interface, a prepared statement is represented by a handle, which is a Pointer object. The life time of a statement generally goes like this:
Prepare the statement with oosqlPrepare, which sets a variable to the handle.
Bind values to host parameters using one of the oosqlBind routines, such as oosqlBindText, oosqlBindInt, or oosqlBindNull.
Execute the SQL by invoking oosqlStep one or more times. Each time oosqlStep returns ROW, the values of the current result row can be retrieved with the oosqlColumn routines, such as oosqlColumnText or oosqlColumnInt.
Possibly, reset the statement using oosqlReset, then go back to step 2. Do this zero or more times.
Release the resources used by the statement by invoking oosqlFinalize.

In SQLite, host parameters and result columns are numbered from 0. In ooSQLite, as is normal in Rexx, they are numbered from 1: the first parameter of a statement and the first column of a result row are number 1.

These are the rules for statement handles. The routines that take a statement as their first argument raise a syntax error, 88.914, if the argument is not a Pointer object, and 88.900 if it is a null handle, which is what oosqlPrepare returns on error, or for SQL text that has no statement. The exceptions are oosqlFinalize, which does nothing for a null handle, and oosqlStmtBusy, which returns false. &changed11;Once a statement has been finalized, its handle is not valid any more, and every routine, also oosqlFinalize, raises 88.900 when it is given it; so does a routine given a handle of another kind, such as a connection. See Handles for the limits of this check. Before ooSQLite 1.1 these handles were not detected, and could crash the interpreter. In the object orientated interface, invoking most methods of an ooSQLiteStmt object that has been finalized raises a syntax error.

Most of the statement routines work like an SQLite API with a similar name, and return what that API returns: a result code for the oosqlBind routines, oosqlStep, oosqlReset, and oosqlFinalize, or the value asked for. The result codes are the ooSQLite Result Code constants, such as .ooSQLite~ROW. When a routine returns an error code, oosqlErrMsg describes the error.

section.title: &changed11;Callback Routines
section.para:
Several routines of the classic interface register a Rexx routine that SQLite calls later, while it executes SQL: a callback routine. They are oosqlBusyHandler, oosqlCollationNeeded, oosqlCommitHook, oosqlCreateCollation, oosqlCreateFunction, oosqlProfile, oosqlProgressHandler, oosqlRollbackHook, oosqlSetAuthorizer, oosqlTrace, and oosqlUpdateHook; oosqlExec can also call a routine for each result row. These are the rules for callback routines:
The routine is given by its name, and it must be a public routine, defined with ::ROUTINE name PUBLIC, in the same program, or package, that calls the registering routine. Public routines of the packages that the program requires are not found. If there is no such routine, a syntax error, 88.900, is raised. Case is not significant in the name.
The empty string as the name removes the routine registered before. The routines are also removed when the connection is closed.
A connection has at most one routine of each kind: registering a routine replaces the one registered before.
The routine is called in the same thread, while the routine that executes the SQL, such as oosqlExec or oosqlStep, is running. Its arguments are described in the section of each registering routine. When a userData object is given to the registering routine, it is passed to the callback routine as its last argument; otherwise that argument is .nil.
The routine must return a whole number, even when its value is ignored. &changed11;If it returns nothing, a syntax error, 44.1, is raised when the routine that executes the SQL returns, and if it returns something else, a syntax error, 98.900. A condition raised in the callback routine is also raised there, as a SYNTAX error: see Callback Methods for how, and for how SQLite stops. Before ooSQLite 1.1 a USER or ERROR condition raised in a callback routine was lost, and a callback routine of oosqlExec that returned nothing, or raised one of them, crashed the interpreter.
Unless its section says otherwise, the routine must not use the database connection: it must not prepare or execute SQL on it.

section.title: Online Backup Feature
section.para: SQLite provides an online backup feature and the classic Rexx interface of ooSQLite provides the functions neccessary to make complete use of this feature. To effectively use the online backup feature with the classic Rexx interface, the Rexx programmer should read the SQLite documentation for the Online Backup API.. SQLite also provides an article with two examples and commentary showing how to use the online backup API. Readers may also find useful the information in the object orientated interface's support for this feature.

These functions in ooSQLite provide the access to the online backup feature of SQLite:
oosqlBackupFinish.
oosqlBackupInit.
oosqlPageCount.
oosqlBackupRemaining.
oosqlBackupStep.
